children.name: pinneapple_core.artifact
children.doc:
``pp.artifact``: the ``.ppx`` container — one file with a result and everything needed to reproduce it.

A ``.ppx`` is a zip holding a JSON manifest and the members that manifest names::

    experiment.ppx
    ├── manifest.json          # schema, problem, units, solver, config, metrics, validation, environment, provenance
    ├── arrays/*.npy           # meshes, fields, datasets, probe points and their expected outputs
    └── model/state.pt         # the weights of the model the artifact carries, when it carries one

The manifest never holds a number that a member does not back: every array and every weight file is listed in
``integrity`` with its sha256, and :func:`load` refuses an artifact whose members do not match what the manifest says.

    import pinneapple as pp

    art = pp.Artifact.from_solution(solution, title="poisson, 32x32")
    pp.save(art, "experiment.ppx")
    same = pp.load("experiment.ppx")           # IntegrityError if a member changed, MissingProvenance if it says nothing
    report = pp.verify_artifact("experiment.ppx")   # integrity, provenance, units, reproduction
    report.passed

**Reproducing on another machine.** An artifact that carries a model records the class and the keyword arguments
that built it (``model/build``) next to the weights, so :meth:`Artifact.predict` and :func:`verify` rebuild the model
from the file alone and compare its outputs to the probe outputs stored with it, within ``rtol``/``atol``.
A solved problem cannot always be re-run from the file — the classical backends take a callable source
(``ctx={"source_fn": ...}``) that no container can carry — so for those the artifact records the problem, the method
and the settings, and :meth:`Artifact.reproduce` accepts the callable that produces the result again, comparing it to
the stored probes rather than pretending it could be rebuilt.

A result plus everything needed to reproduce it.

Every field is JSON-safe except ``arrays`` and ``model_state``: the first holds the ``.npy`` members by name, the
second the weights. ``reproductions`` names, for each probe set, the array with the inputs, the array with the
outputs that were produced, and the tolerance under which a re-run is the same result.

functions.name: compatibility
functions.doc:
Can this version read an artifact with this manifest, and what should the reader know (#225)?

Two questions, kept apart. The **schema** decides what is readable: the same version reads, an older one reads
through the migration registered for it, an older one with no migration and a newer one are refused with the
reason and the way out. The **library version** that wrote it decides what to warn about: the same major reads,
a different major is refused (the numbers may come from a different solver), and the schema is what decides the
rest — a warning is not a refusal, it is a note the caller can see.

functions.name: save
functions.sig: (artifact: Any, path: str | os.PathLike[str], *, title: str | None = None, units: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, samples: int = 0, seed: int = 0, init_kwargs: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, config: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, **kwargs) -> Path
functions.doc:
Write ``artifact`` as a ``.ppx`` file and return its path (the extension is added when missing).

Accepts an :class:`Artifact`, a ``Solution`` from ``pp.solve`` or a torch model; the keyword arguments are what
the matching constructor needs (``samples`` stores probe points for the reproduction).

functions.name: load
functions.sig: (path: str | os.PathLike[str], *, verify: bool = True, strict: bool = True) -> Artifact
functions.doc:
Read a ``.ppx`` back into an :class:`Artifact`.

``verify`` checks every member against the sha256 in the manifest (``IntegrityError`` when one changed);
``strict`` refuses an artifact whose provenance block is absent or incomplete (``MissingProvenance``), which is
what keeps an anonymous number from travelling as a result.

functions.name: verify
functions.sig: (path: str | os.PathLike[str], *, reproduce: bool = True, rtol: float | None = None, atol: float | None = None, predict_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray] | None = None) -> Report
functions.doc:
Everything that can be checked about a file without trusting it: the manifest, the members, the provenance,
the units and, when the artifact carries a model (or ``predict_fn`` is given), a reproduction.

children.name: pinneapple_core.backend
children.doc:
PhysicsBackend: one array/derivative/solve API over torch, jax and anything registered.

Code written against a :class:`PhysicsBackend` does not name an engine::

    from pinneapple_core.backend import get_physics_backend

    def energy(bk, L):                        # bk is the active backend
        x = bk.linspace(0.0, L, 101)
        return bk.integrate(bk.sin(x) ** 2, x)

    bk = get_physics_backend()
    dE = bk.grad(lambda L: energy(bk, L))(bk.asarray(2.0))

``pp.set_backend("jax")`` (or ``with use_backend("jax"):``) switches the engine, and the same function
returns the same numbers. Float64 is the default dtype so results agree across engines.

Operations: ``asarray, to_numpy, linspace, zeros, ones, eye, diag, matmul, solve, integrate`` and the
transforms ``grad, jacobian, vmap, jit`` (``jit`` is a no-op where the engine has none). Elementwise
functions (``sin, exp, sum, stack, where, ...``) live on ``bk.xp``, the engine's own numpy-like module.

Add an engine with ``register_backend("name", MyBackend)``; ``MyBackend`` subclasses :class:`PhysicsBackend`.

children.name: pinneapple_core.catalog
children.doc:
One catalogue over everything the library can list (#1478).

Before this module there were five lists that did not know about each other: ``pp.list_models()``, the registry
gateway's models, the benchmark's suites, the app's model catalogue and the arena's. A model available in one was
not necessarily available in the others, and nothing said so — a benchmark could score a subset of what the app
advertised, with no error anywhere.

``pp.catalog()`` is a **read-only** facade over the unified registry (#200). It does not add a sixth list: every
section reads ``pp.registered(kind)`` and ``registry.describe(name)``, which is the one source of truth. Writes go
to the registry, through ``pp.register``.

What it adds on top of the registry is the part the registry cannot say by itself:

* **one entry shape** — ``id``, ``kind``, ``title``, plus ``units``, ``variables`` and ``provenance`` that are
  ``None`` when the registration did not declare them. A missing field is never filled with a default that looks
  like data;
* **the views** — every list that a user or another component reads, with the set of ids each one reports;
* **the discrepancies** — ids that one view lists and another does not. A view that is a different plane on purpose
  (the registry gateway holds *trained* artifacts, not architectures) says so in one sentence instead of being
  silently tolerated.

Example
-------
>>> import pinneapple as pp
>>> catalogue = pp.catalog()
>>> len(catalogue.models()) > 0
True
>>> catalogue.get("vanilla_pinn").kind
'model'
>>> catalogue.discrepancies()["models"]          # empty when every architecture view agrees
[]

classes.doc: One catalogue entry: what it is, and the fields it declared — ``None`` where it declared nothing.

classes.name: CatalogView
classes.doc:
A list somebody reads, and whether it is supposed to agree with the catalogue.

``note`` is ``None`` for a view that lists the same resources as the catalogue — a disagreement is then a bug.
When the view is a **different plane** (trained artifacts, a benchmark's own suite), ``note`` says so in one
sentence, so the difference is a stated fact rather than a silent tolerance.

children.name: pinneapple_core.data
children.doc:
Physics-native data API: ``PhysicsDataset``, ``DataLoader`` and the samplers.

One loader serves a PINN, a neural operator and an inverse problem. A loader takes *sources*, each either a
:class:`PhysicsDataset` (labelled arrays, shuffled and batched) or a :class:`Sampler` (points drawn on demand),
and yields a :class:`Batch` with one group per source::

    loader = DataLoader({"col": CollocationSampler(domain), "bc": BoundarySampler(geometry),
                         "obs": PhysicsDataset(x_obs, u_obs)},
                        batch_size={"col": 1024, "bc": 128, "obs": 16}, steps=2000)
    for batch in loader:
        x = batch["col"]["x"]                  # requires_grad already set: collocation points are differentiated
        ...

Samplers: :class:`CollocationSampler` (interior, uniform / lhs / sobol), :class:`BoundarySampler` (boundary points with
outward normals, whole boundary or a named part), :class:`MeshSampler` (nodes, cell centres or random points in cells),
:class:`TrajectorySampler` (windows of time series), :class:`AdaptiveSampler` (density follows the PDE residual) and
:class:`ActiveSampler` (picks the highest-scoring candidates by an acquisition function).
``physics_aware=True`` (the default) makes the loader set ``requires_grad`` on the points of sources that need
derivatives, convert to the model dtype and device, and attach the coordinate names to ``batch.meta``.

classes.name: Batch
classes.doc: One training step's data: ``batch["col"]["x"]``. With a single source, ``batch.x`` and ``batch.y`` shortcut it.

classes.name: PhysicsDataset
classes.sig: (inputs, targets = None, *, coords: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, fields: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, domain: Optional[Domain] = None, name: str = '', provenance: Optional[Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]]] = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Labelled samples ``inputs[i] -> targets[i]`` plus the physics context: coordinate and field names, domain.

``inputs`` / ``targets`` are arrays or tensors with the sample index first. For a PINN's observations ``inputs`` are
the coordinates; for an operator they are the input functions on a grid.

methods.name: split
methods.doc: Random split, e.g. ``split([0.8, 0.2])``; fractions must sum to 1.

classes.name: Sampler
classes.doc: Draws points on demand. Subclasses implement :meth:`sample` and return a dict of tensors with key ``"x"``.

methods.name: update
methods.doc: Hook called by ``DataLoader.update(model)`` for samplers that adapt to the model.

classes.name: CollocationSampler
classes.sig: (domain, strategy: str = 'uniform', seed: int = 0) -> None
classes.doc:
Interior points for the PDE residual. ``domain``: a ``Domain``, a ``Geometry`` or ``{"x": (0, 1), "t": (0, 1)}``.
``strategy``: ``uniform``, ``lhs`` (Latin hypercube) or ``sobol``. Every call draws fresh points, reproducibly from ``seed``.

classes.name: BoundarySampler
classes.sig: (domain, part: Optional[str] = None, seed: int = 0) -> None
classes.doc:
Boundary points with outward unit normals (``"x"``, ``"normal"``). With a ``Geometry``, ``part="x_min"`` samples
one named boundary. Normals are needed by Neumann conditions, so the points are differentiable by default.

classes.name: MeshSampler
classes.sig: (mesh: Mesh, mode: str = 'nodes', seed: int = 0) -> None
classes.doc:
Points tied to a mesh: ``mode="nodes"`` (random nodes, or all when ``n >= N``), ``"cells"`` (cell centres) or
``"random"`` (uniform points inside cells, by volume). Returns ``x`` and the node or cell index.

classes.name: TrajectorySampler
classes.sig: (states, n_in: int = 1, n_out: int = 1, stride: int = 1, seed: int = 0) -> None
classes.doc:
Windows of trajectories ``states (B, T, d)``: ``x`` is ``n_in`` consecutive states, ``y`` the next ``n_out``.
For learning dynamics, one-step maps and rollouts. Returns ``x (n, n_in, d)``, ``y (n, n_out, d)``, ``t0`` (start index).

classes.name: AdaptiveSampler
classes.sig: (base: Sampler, residual_fn: Callable, pool_size: int = 20000, exponent: float = 1.0, uniform_fraction: float = 0.2, seed: int = 0) -> None
classes.doc:
Residual-based adaptive sampling: a pool of candidates from ``base``; after ``update(model)`` the points are drawn
with probability proportional to ``residual ** exponent`` (mixed with ``uniform_fraction`` of uniform draws so no
region is abandoned). ``residual_fn(model, x) -> (P,)`` gives non-negative magnitudes. Before the first update it is
uniform over the pool.

classes.name: ActiveSampler
classes.sig: (base: Sampler, score_fn: Callable, n_candidates: int = 2000) -> None
classes.doc:
Acquisition-driven selection: draw ``n_candidates`` from ``base`` and return the ``n`` with the highest
``score_fn(model, x)`` (uncertainty, ensemble variance, expected information, ...). Use it to choose where to run
the next expensive simulation or experiment. Differs from :class:`AdaptiveSampler`, which samples *proportionally*.

classes.name: DataLoader
classes.sig: (sources, batch_size: Union[int, Mapping[str, int]] = 256, steps: Optional[int] = None, shuffle: bool = True, drop_last: bool = False, seed: int = 0, physics_aware: bool = True, device = None, dtype = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Batches from datasets and samplers behind one iteration API.

Args:
    sources: a :class:`PhysicsDataset`, a :class:`Sampler`, or ``{name: source}``.
    batch_size: an int for every source, or ``{name: int}``.
    steps: number of batches. Optional when there is a dataset: then one pass over the *first* dataset
        (``ceil(len / batch_size)`` batches) is one epoch. Required when every source is a sampler.
    shuffle: reshuffle datasets each epoch. ``drop_last``: drop the last short dataset batch.
    physics_aware: set ``requires_grad`` on the points of sources that are differentiated (collocation, boundary,
        adaptive), convert to ``dtype`` / ``device``, add ``meta["coords"]``.

methods.name: update
methods.doc: Tell adaptive and active samplers about the current model (call every few steps).

children.name: pinneapple_core.distributed
children.doc:
``pp.distributed``: run physics workloads in parallel, not only training.

* **Experiments and ensembles**: :func:`map`, :func:`sweep`, :func:`ensemble` run a function over many inputs in worker processes
  (or threads) and return the results in input order, with errors collected per task instead of lost.
* **Meshes**: :func:`partition_mesh` splits a mesh into parts with one layer of halo cells, so a per-part computation of a nodal
  quantity (gradients, integrals) equals the global one; :func:`map_mesh` runs it on all parts and gathers.
* **Domains**: :func:`decompose_box` and :func:`train_decomposed` train a PINN by additive Schwarz iteration: the box is cut into
  overlapping subdomains, each trained in its own worker against the interface values of its neighbours from the previous
  iteration, so the subdomains of one iteration run concurrently.

>>> import pinneapple_core.distributed as dist
>>> dist.map(lambda k: k * k, range(5), workers=1)
[0, 1, 4, 9, 16]

``backend="process"`` uses joblib's loky pool when joblib is installed (closures and lambdas are fine) and
``concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor`` otherwise (functions must then be importable). ``"thread"`` suits numpy/torch code that
releases the GIL, ``"serial"`` runs in the caller (useful to debug). Data-parallel gradient averaging across devices
(``torch.distributed``) is not part of this module.

classes.name: TaskError
classes.doc: A failed task, returned in place of its result when ``errors="collect"``.

classes.name: SweepResult
classes.doc: Records of a parameter sweep: one per configuration, in grid order.

methods.name: best
methods.sig: (key: Callable[[Any], float] = lambda r: r, minimize: bool = True) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc: The successful record whose ``key(result)`` is smallest (largest with ``minimize=False``).

methods.name: table
methods.doc: Flat rows ``{**params, "result": ..., "error": ..., "time_s": ...}``.

classes.name: MeshPart
classes.doc:
One part of a partitioned mesh: the local mesh (owned cells plus a halo layer), the global ids of its nodes and cells,
and which local nodes this part owns (each global node is owned by exactly one part).

classes.name: Subdomain
classes.doc: A box ``[lo, hi]`` that overlaps its neighbours; ``core`` is the part it owns when predicting.

methods.name: predict
methods.doc: Each point is evaluated by the subdomain that owns it (its core).

functions.name: map
functions.sig: (fn: Callable[[Any], Any], items: Iterable[Any], workers: int | None = None, *, backend: str = 'process', errors: str = 'raise', chunksize: int = 1) -> list[Any]
functions.doc:
``[fn(x) for x in items]`` on ``workers`` workers (default: the CPU count), in input order.

``errors="raise"`` re-raises the first failure; ``errors="collect"`` returns a :class:`TaskError` in the failed slots.

functions.name: sweep
functions.sig: (fn: Callable[..., Any], grid: Mapping[str, Sequence[Any]] | Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]], workers: int | None = None, *, backend: str = 'process', chunksize: int = 1) -> SweepResult
functions.doc:
Run ``fn(**params)`` for every configuration: the Cartesian product of a ``{name: values}`` grid, or an explicit list of
dicts. Failures are recorded (``record["error"]``), never raised, so one bad configuration does not lose the sweep.

functions.name: ensemble
functions.sig: (fn: Callable[..., Any], n: int, workers: int | None = None, *, seed: int = 0, backend: str = 'process') -> list[Any]
functions.doc:
``n`` independent runs ``fn(seed=s_i)`` with statistically independent seeds spawned from ``seed``
(``numpy.random.SeedSequence``), reproducible whatever the number of workers.

functions.name: partition_mesh
functions.doc:
Split ``mesh`` into ``n_parts`` by recursive coordinate bisection of the cell centres, each part getting close to an
equal share of the cells, and adding every cell that shares a node with an owned cell (one halo layer). A nodal operator
that needs the cells around a node (gradient recovery, an integral assembled per node) is then exact on the owned nodes
of each part.

functions.name: map_mesh
functions.sig: (fn: Callable[[Any, np.ndarray], np.ndarray], mesh, values: np.ndarray, n_parts: int, workers: int | None = None, *, backend: str = 'process') -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Apply a nodal operator in parallel. ``fn(local_mesh, local_values) -> (n_local_nodes, ...)`` runs on every part (with its
halo); the rows of the owned nodes are gathered into one global array of shape ``(N, ...)``.

functions.name: decompose_box
functions.sig: (lo: Sequence[float], hi: Sequence[float], parts: int, overlap: float = 0.1, axis: int = 0) -> list[Subdomain]
functions.doc:
Cut the box into ``parts`` strips along ``axis``, each extended by ``overlap`` (a fraction of the strip width) into its
neighbours. Overlap is what lets additive Schwarz converge.

functions.name: train_decomposed
functions.sig: (residual: Callable, boundary: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], make_model: Callable[[], Any], lo: Sequence[float], hi: Sequence[float], parts: int = 4, overlap: float = 0.25, iterations: int = 6, steps: int = 400, workers: int | None = None, *, n_col: int = 256, n_bc: int = 32, lr: float = 0.003, w_bc: float = 20.0, axis: int = 0, seed: int = 0, backend: str = 'process', reference: Callable...
functions.doc:
Train a PINN on a box by additive Schwarz iteration.

Each iteration trains every subdomain network for ``steps`` Adam steps, all subdomains concurrently, against the PDE residual
inside it, the boundary condition ``boundary(X) -> values`` on the faces that lie on the true boundary, and the neighbours'
previous-iteration predictions on the interface faces. ``residual(model, x) -> tensor`` must differentiate ``model(x)`` with
respect to ``x`` (``x.requires_grad`` is set). With ``reference`` the history records the relative L2 error after every iteration.

children.name: pinneapple_core.domain
children.doc:
Domain: the region of space a problem lives on.

A :class:`Domain` is an axis-aligned bounding box, optionally cut down by a
signed distance function (negative inside). It answers the three questions a
solver asks of its region: is this point inside, give me points inside, give me
points on the boundary. Boxes work in any dimension; irregular domains come from
the CSG shapes of :mod:`pinneapple_design.geometry.csg` (2D).

>>> from pinneapple_core import Domain
>>> d = Domain.box([0, 0], [2, 1])
>>> d.volume()
2.0
>>> d.sample_interior(128, seed=0).shape
(128, 2)

children.name: pinneapple_core.errors
children.doc:
Errors that teach: every message says what broke *and* what to do about it (#46, roadmap A5).

A bare ``ValueError("repeats must be >= 1")`` tells a user that they were wrong and leaves them to guess what
"right" looks like. The errors here carry a second half -- the action -- and every one of them renders as::

    repeats must be >= 1
      Fix: pass repeats=5 (the default) or any integer >= 1
      See: docs/dev/errors_that_teach.md

Three things follow from that shape:

- the *type* is unchanged where it matters: each class also inherits the standard exception a caller already
  catches (``BadValue`` is a ``ValueError``, ``MissingExtra`` an ``ImportError``, ``UnknownName`` a ``KeyError``,
  ``NotConfigured`` a ``RuntimeError``, ``NotSupported`` a ``NotImplementedError``), so ``except ValueError`` keeps
  working and nobody's error handling breaks because a message got better;
- the action is data (``err.fix``), not prose buried in a string, so a tool can group failures by remedy and the
  audit below can be checked mechanically;
- raising one is one line: ``raise BadValue("what broke", fix="what to do")``.

The audit -- the 30 most common errors a user of this library actually hits -- lives in :data:`AUDITED` and is
rendered into ``docs/dev/errors_that_teach.md`` by :func:`audit_markdown`. Each entry names the site, the failure,
and the sentence that now tells the user what to do; ``tests/test_errors_that_teach.py`` triggers every one of them
and refuses an entry whose error does not carry a fix, which is what keeps this file honest instead of decorative.

What counts as teachable, and what does not: a message names an *action* when the user can take it (install the
extra, pass a valid argument, call ``fit`` first, widen the budget). It is not an action to say "invalid input" or
to list the valid values without saying which call takes them. Internal invariant failures (``assert``-style
"this should never happen") are out of scope: there is nothing for the user to do.

children.name: pinneapple_core.fem
children.doc:
Differentiable P1 finite elements on simplex meshes.

Everything here is written in torch, so the solution of a PDE is differentiable with respect to the
**vertex coordinates**, which is the mesh (shape) gradient. Parametrise the geometry as
``points = f(design_parameters)`` and ``loss.backward()`` returns d(objective)/d(design_parameters).
The linear solve is :func:`torch.linalg.solve`, whose backward pass is the adjoint solve.

Matrices are dense, so this is meant for meshes up to a few thousand nodes: reference cases, shape
optimisation prototypes and tests of larger solvers.

>>> import numpy as np, torch
>>> from pinneapple_core import Mesh
>>> from pinneapple_core.fem import solve_poisson
>>> m = Mesh.interval(0.0, 1.0, 20)
>>> pts = torch.tensor(m.points, dtype=torch.float64)
>>> u = solve_poisson(pts, m.cells, 1.0, m.boundary_nodes())
>>> round(float(u.max()), 4)   # -u'' = 1 on (0,1), exact max 1/8
0.125

children.name: pinneapple_core.field
children.doc:
Field: values of a physical quantity on a grid, a mesh or a point cloud.

A :class:`Field` ties values to the space they live on, so the same four calls
work on every discretisation::

    f.gradient()         # derivative, as a Field on the same support
    f.divergence()       # trace of the gradient of a vector field
    f.interpolate(x)     # values at arbitrary points
    f.integrate()        # integral over the support

Values have shape ``(N, *components)``: ``(N,)`` for a scalar, ``(N, d)`` for a
vector, ``(N, c, d)`` for a gradient of a vector. :class:`FunctionField` is the
same interface for a callable (an analytic expression or a neural network) with
derivatives from autograd, which is what a PINN needs.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from pinneapple_core import Field
>>> x = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
>>> f = Field.on_grid([x], np.sin(np.pi * x))
>>> round(float(f.integrate()), 3)
0.637

children.name: pinneapple_core.func
children.doc:
``pp.func``: function transforms with scientific semantics, and implicit differentiation.

Two things live here.

**Transforms** wrap :mod:`torch.func` (``grad, jacobian, jacrev, jacfwd, hessian, vmap``) and add
``wrt``: the argument to differentiate, by name or position. A model written as
``model(geometry, mu)`` is differentiated with respect to its geometry with
``jacobian(model, wrt="geometry")``; several arguments return a tuple.

**Implicit differentiation** (:func:`implicit_solve`) gives gradients through a solver call
without differentiating the solver's iterations. If ``x*(theta)`` solves
``residual(x, theta) = 0``, then ``dx*/dtheta = -(dF/dx)^-1 dF/dtheta``; the backward pass is one
linear (adjoint) solve, whatever the forward solver did, including an external code.

>>> import torch
>>> from pinneapple_core import func
>>> f = lambda x, mu: (mu * x ** 2).sum()
>>> func.grad(f, wrt="mu")(torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0]), torch.tensor(3.0)).item()
5.0

functions.name: grad
functions.sig: (fn: Callable, wrt: Wrt = 0, *, has_aux: bool = False) -> Callable
functions.doc: Gradient of a scalar-valued ``fn`` with respect to the argument(s) ``wrt``.

functions.name: jacrev
functions.sig: (fn: Callable, wrt: Wrt = 0, *, has_aux: bool = False) -> Callable
functions.doc: Jacobian by reverse mode: cheap when ``fn`` has few outputs.

functions.name: jacfwd
functions.sig: (fn: Callable, wrt: Wrt = 0, *, has_aux: bool = False) -> Callable
functions.doc: Jacobian by forward mode: cheap when ``fn`` has few inputs.

functions.name: jacobian
functions.sig: (fn: Callable, wrt: Wrt = 0, *, mode: str = 'auto') -> Callable
functions.doc:
Jacobian of ``fn`` with respect to ``wrt``. ``mode`` is ``"rev"``, ``"fwd"`` or
``"auto"`` (forward when the argument has fewer entries than the output has).

functions.name: hessian
functions.doc: Hessian of a scalar-valued ``fn`` with respect to ``wrt``.

functions.name: vmap
functions.doc: Vectorise ``fn`` over a batch dimension (``torch.func.vmap``).

functions.name: newton_solve
functions.sig: (residual: Callable[..., Tensor], x0: Tensor, *params, tol: float = 1e-10, max_iter: int = 50) -> Tensor
functions.doc:
Damped Newton iteration for ``residual(x, *params) = 0`` with a dense Jacobian.

Not differentiable by design (it runs under ``no_grad``); use :func:`implicit_solve` to
differentiate through it. Raises ``RuntimeError`` if it does not converge.

functions.name: implicit_solve
functions.sig: (residual: Callable[..., Tensor], x0: Tensor, *params, solver: Optional[Callable[..., Tensor]] = None, tol: float = 1e-10, max_iter: int = 50) -> Tensor
functions.doc:
Solve ``residual(x, *params) = 0`` for ``x`` and differentiate through the solution.

Gradients with respect to ``params`` come from the implicit function theorem,
``dx*/dp = -(dF/dx)^-1 dF/dp``, so the cost of the backward pass is one adjoint linear
solve and does not depend on how many iterations the forward solver took.

Args:
    residual: ``residual(x, *params)``, same shape as ``x``, differentiable in ``x`` and ``params``.
    x0: initial guess (also fixes the shape of the solution).
    params: tensors the solution depends on.
    solver: optional forward solver ``solver(residual, x0, *params) -> x*``, for example a
        call to an external code. It is never differentiated. Default: damped Newton.

Gradients are exact to first order (reverse or forward mode). The Jacobian ``dF/dx`` is dense
and size ``(x.numel())**2``; second derivatives through the solve ignore its dependence on ``params``.

children.name: pinneapple_core.loss
children.doc:
``pp.loss``: functional loss terms and a balancer selectable by name.

Terms are plain functions returning a scalar tensor::

    pde(residual)                     mean squared PDE residual (optionally causal)
    boundary(pred, target)            boundary / initial condition mismatch
    conservation(quantity, target)    a conserved quantity or a divergence-free constraint
    energy(e, mode=...)               energy conserved, or not increasing
    symmetry(model, x, transform)     invariance / equivariance under a transformation
    supervised(pred, target, kind)    data fit: mse, mae, huber, relative_l2
    inverse(pred, observed, params)   data misfit plus a prior on the unknown parameters

``combine(terms, weights)`` sums them. For weights that change during training build a
:class:`Balancer` with a strategy name::

    total = pp.loss.combine({"pde": pde(r), "bc": boundary(u_b, g)}, {"pde": 1.0, "bc": 10.0})

    balancer = pp.loss.Balancer("gradnorm", names=["pde", "bc"], model=net)
    total = balancer({"pde": pde(r), "bc": boundary(u_b, g)}, step=i)
    total.backward()

``Balancer.strategies()`` lists the names: the fixed and learned weights, GradNorm, NTK, ReLoBRaLo,
SoftAdapt, augmented Lagrangian, inverse-Dirichlet, learning-rate annealing, PCGrad, an automatic switcher,
and ``"curriculum"`` (weights ramped over the first steps). Causal training of time-dependent residuals is
``pde(residual, t=t, causal_epsilon=...)``.

classes.name: Balancer
classes.sig: (strategy: str = 'fixed', names: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, model: Optional[torch.nn.Module] = None, weights: Optional[Mapping[str, float]] = None, update_every: int = 100, *, schedule: Optional[Mapping[str, Tuple[float, float]]] = None, steps: int = 1000, shape: str = 'linear', **options) -> None
classes.doc:
Loss weighting chosen by name. Call it with the dict of terms to get the weighted total.

Args:
    strategy: one of :func:`list_strategies`.
    names: the term names, e.g. ``["pde", "bc", "ic"]``; calling with other names raises.
    model: the network, needed by the strategies that read gradients (``gradnorm``, ``ntk``,
        ``inverse_dirichlet``, ``lr_annealing``, ``pcgrad``, ``auto``).
    weights: starting (or fixed) weight per term, default 1.
    update_every: steps between weight updates for the strategies that update periodically.
    schedule / steps / shape: for ``"curriculum"``, ``{"bc": (start, end)}`` ramped over ``steps`` steps
        (``shape`` is ``linear`` or ``cosine``); terms not in the schedule keep ``weights``.
    options: forwarded to the strategy's configuration (``alpha``, ``lr``, ``clip_min``, ``clip_max``, ``tau``, ...).

methods.name: weights
methods.doc: The weights applied at the last call (the starting weights before any call).

methods.name: history
methods.doc: Weight applied to each term at every call (where the strategy records it).

methods.name: weight_parameters
methods.doc: Learnable weights (``self_adaptive``): optimise them by gradient *ascent*, see the example. Empty otherwise.

functions.name: causal_weights
functions.sig: (residual: Tensor, t: Tensor, n_chunks: int = 32, epsilon: float = 1.0) -> Tensor
functions.doc:
Per-point causal weights ``exp(-epsilon * sum of the mean squared residual of earlier time chunks)``
(Wang et al. 2022), detached. ``t`` must be normalised to [0, 1].

functions.name: pde
functions.sig: (residual: Tensor, *, weights: Optional[Tensor] = None, t: Optional[Tensor] = None, causal_epsilon: Optional[float] = None, n_chunks: int = 32) -> Tensor
functions.doc:
Mean squared residual. ``weights`` (one per point) gives a weighted mean ``sum(w r^2) / sum(w)``;
``t`` with ``causal_epsilon`` computes causal weights from the residual itself.

functions.name: boundary
functions.doc: Mean squared mismatch with the prescribed boundary or initial values.

functions.name: supervised
functions.sig: (pred: Tensor, target: Tensor, kind: str = 'mse', *, delta: float = 1.0) -> Tensor
functions.doc:
Data fit. ``kind``: ``mse``, ``mae``, ``huber`` (``delta``) or ``relative_l2`` (norm of the error over
the norm of the target, over the whole batch).

functions.name: conservation
functions.sig: (quantity: Tensor, target: Union[Tensor, float] = 0.0, scale: Optional[float] = None) -> Tensor
functions.doc:
Squared deviation of a conserved ``quantity`` (total mass, a flux balance, a divergence) from ``target``,
divided by ``scale`` when the quantity is not O(1).

functions.name: energy
functions.sig: (e: Tensor, reference: Union[Tensor, float, None] = None, mode: str = 'conserve') -> Tensor
functions.doc:
Energy along time, ``e`` of shape ``(T,)`` or ``(T, ...)`` ordered in time.

* ``conserve``: mean squared deviation from ``reference`` (default: the first value).
* ``nonincrease``: penalises rises, ``mean(relu(e[k+1] - e[k])^2)`` (dissipative systems).
* ``nondecrease``: penalises drops (growth, accumulation).

functions.name: symmetry
functions.sig: (model: Callable[[Tensor], Tensor], x: Tensor, transform: Callable[[Tensor], Tensor], output_transform: Optional[Callable[[Tensor], Tensor]] = None) -> Tensor
functions.doc:
Penalty for breaking a symmetry: ``mean((f(T x) - S f(x))^2)``. ``S`` is ``output_transform``
(identity by default, which is invariance; a rotation of a vector output makes it equivariance).

functions.name: inverse
functions.sig: (pred: Tensor, observed: Tensor, params: Optional[Union[Tensor, Iterable[Tensor]]] = None, prior: Union[Tensor, float, None] = None, reg: float = 0.0) -> Tensor
functions.doc: Misfit to the observations plus ``reg * mean((params - prior)^2)`` on the unknown parameters (prior 0 by default).

functions.name: combine
functions.sig: (terms: Mapping[str, Tensor], weights: Optional[Mapping[str, float]] = None) -> Tensor
functions.doc:
Weighted sum of named terms (weight 1 where not given). Weights for terms that are absent raise
``KeyError``: a misspelt name must not silently drop a loss term.

children.name: pinneapple_core.module
children.doc:
PhysicsModule: composable models and solvers, the ``nn.Module`` of physics.

Everything is a torch module with a ``kind``, so a neural network, a numerical solver and a mix of the two
compose with the same few classes::

    import torch.nn as nn
    from pinneapple_core.module import Hybrid, SolverModule

    coarse = SolverModule(coarse_fem_solve)                       # any differentiable function, or a pp.solve method
    model = Hybrid(coarse, nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 32), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(32, 1)), mode="residual")
    model.fit(x, y, epochs=200)                                  # trains the corrector through the solver

* :class:`PhysicsModule`  base class: ``describe()``, ``num_parameters()``, a small ``fit``.
* :class:`Sequential`     chain components, each feeding the next.
* :class:`SolverModule`   a solver as a component: ``fn`` (autograd flows through it), optional trainable
  parameters, or :meth:`SolverModule.from_method` for any ``pp.solve`` backend (not differentiable).
* :class:`Hybrid`         solver output combined with a neural correction.

methods.sig: (x, y, *, epochs: int = 200, lr: float = 0.01, loss_fn: Optional[Callable] = None, batch_size: Optional[int] = None, optimizer: Optional[torch.optim.Optimizer] = None, seed: int = 0, verbose: bool = False) -> List[float]
methods.doc:
Minimal training loop on ``(x, y)`` (tensors, or a tuple of tensors for ``x``). Returns the loss per epoch.
Gradients reach every trainable parameter, including those of solver components.

classes.name: Lambda
classes.sig: (fn: Callable) -> None
classes.doc: Wrap a plain function (no parameters) as a component.

classes.name: Sequential
classes.sig: (*parts) -> None
classes.doc:
Chain components: the output of each is the input of the next. Accepts modules, solvers and plain
functions; pass ``(name, module)`` pairs or an ``OrderedDict`` to name them.

classes.name: SolverModule
classes.sig: (fn: Callable, params: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None, trainable: Iterable[str] = (), name: Optional[str] = None) -> None
classes.doc:
A solver as a component.

``fn(*inputs, **params)`` is any torch function, for example a differentiable finite-element solve; autograd
flows through it to its inputs and to the parameters. ``params`` are tensors passed to ``fn`` by keyword; the
names in ``trainable`` become ``nn.Parameter`` (identification, calibration), the rest buffers.

For solvers that are not differentiable (an external code, any ``pp.solve`` method) use
:meth:`from_method`: the output is a constant for autograd, so only components after it train.

methods.name: from_method
methods.doc:
Component from a ``pp.solve`` method: solves ``problem`` once and evaluates the solution at the points
it is called with (``X`` of shape ``(N, n_coords)``, tensor or array). Not differentiable.

classes.name: Hybrid
classes.sig: (solver: Union[nn.Module, Callable], corrector: Union[nn.Module, Callable], mode: str = 'residual', corrector_input: Optional[Callable[[Tuple[Any, ...], Tensor], Tensor]] = None, detach_solver: bool = False) -> None
classes.doc:
A solver plus a neural correction.

``u0 = solver(*inputs)``; the corrector sees ``corrector_input(inputs, u0)`` (default: ``u0``) and the output is

* ``"residual"``       ``u0 + corrector(...)``        learn what the solver misses
* ``"multiplicative"`` ``u0 * (1 + corrector(...))``  learn a relative error
* ``"replace"``        ``corrector(...)``             the solver only supplies features

``detach_solver=True`` stops gradients into the solver (cheaper when it has nothing to learn).
``forward(..., return_parts=True)`` returns ``{"solver", "correction", "output"}`` for diagnostics.

children.summary: PhysicsModule: composable models and solvers, the nn.Module of physics.

children.name: pinneapple_core.onboarding
pinneapple_core.onboarding.catalog
children.doc:
The preset catalogue: what a preset takes, what it gives back, and the smallest program that uses it.

The preset registry (``pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.presets``) stores a factory per name and
nothing else: no description, no tags, no audience. That is fine for the solvers and useless for a
person choosing what to run. This module adds the missing half, derived from the live
:class:`~pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.spec.ProblemSpec` where the spec can answer and curated
by hand where it cannot:

* :func:`card` — one preset as a :class:`Card`: coordinates, fields, conditions, the method that
  runs today, and a snippet that executes as printed.
* :func:`search` — free text, English or Portuguese, to presets, with the terms that matched.
* :func:`snippet` — the smallest correct program for one preset, choosing a method that exists.

Everything here runs offline and without training. ``search`` is keyword scoring, not a model, and
it says so: every hit carries the terms that matched so the user can judge it.

classes.name: Card
classes.doc: One preset as a person needs it: what it is, what goes in, what comes out, how to run it.

methods.name: format
methods.doc: The card as text, ready to print.

functions.name: best_method
functions.doc:
The cheapest method that actually runs for this preset today: analytic, else the reference
solver, else a trained network. Chosen from what the library registers and what this machine
has, not from a table.

functions.name: needs_geometry_tags
functions.doc:
True when the preset binds its boundary conditions to named geometry tags, so a bare
``pp.solve(name, method="pinn")`` cannot build the problem: the tags have to be supplied.

functions.name: tag_names
functions.doc: The geometry tags a preset's conditions refer to, for the message that asks for them.

functions.name: default_geometry_note
functions.doc: Which canonical geometry the preset supplies for its tagged boundaries, or ``""``.

functions.name: trainable
functions.doc:
Can a network be trained on this preset with nothing but its name?

A preset that binds its boundaries to geometry tags can, when it declares its own box or cylinder
for those tags (``pde_environment/presets/tag_geometry.py``): ``pp.solve`` sends that geometry
automatically. When it does not, the tags have to come from the user's mesh.

functions.name: probe
functions.doc:
Try the cheapest method for this preset once and report whether it worked, with the reason.

Cached per process. Only pure-library solvers are attempted: an OpenFOAM or FEniCS campaign is
never started from a card, its presence is checked instead. When the classical solver refuses a
problem it does not cover and the preset can be trained instead (including its own geometry for
tagged boundaries), this returns success and records ``pinn`` as the method that works: what the
card then prints is what will run, not what the preset would prefer.

functions.name: runnable
functions.doc:
True when this preset produces a field on this machine right now, without the user adding
geometry or installing a solver.

functions.name: working_method
functions.doc: The method that works here for this preset: the probed one after a fallback, else the preferred.

functions.name: solver_available
functions.doc:
Can this machine run the named reference solver right now?

A solver is present when any of its probes is: an importable module, or an executable on PATH
(``bin:<program>``). For OpenFOAM that means the solvers themselves, not the ``openfoam``
launcher, which exists on a machine whose environment was never sourced.

functions.name: solver_requirement
functions.doc: The install command for a reference solver this machine does not have, or ``""``.

functions.name: snippet
functions.sig: (name: str, method: Optional[str] = None, *, train: bool = False) -> str
functions.doc:
The smallest correct program for one preset. Runs as printed: no placeholders to fill in.

Two things the program never does: pretend a method this machine cannot run will work, and fail
without saying why. When the classical solver refuses a problem it does not cover, the program
trains instead and prints which method actually ran. When training also needs something the
user has to supply (a geometry with named tags), the program says what, before it runs.

functions.name: standalone_snippet
functions.doc:
A program that solves the same physics as this preset, described from scratch.

Presets that bind their boundaries to geometry tags, or whose solver is not installed, cannot be
solved from their name alone. The equation, the fields and the coefficients still can: this
writes the same PDE on a box with Dirichlet boundaries, which trains anywhere. Returns ``""``
when the preset's PDE kind is not one the compiler handles, because printing a program that
cannot run is worse than printing nothing.

functions.name: card
functions.sig: (name: str, *, with_related: bool = True, check: bool = True) -> Card
functions.doc:
Describe one preset. Raises ``KeyError`` for an unknown name, with the near misses.

With ``check`` (the default) the card tries the cheapest method once, so ``available`` and
``error`` say whether this preset really produces a field on this machine, rather than assuming
it. Cheap solvers are tried; an external one is checked for presence and never started.

functions.name: describe
functions.doc: ``card(name)`` as a JSON-friendly dict.

functions.name: catalogue
functions.doc: Every registered preset as a card, sorted by domain then name.

functions.name: domains
functions.doc: Preset names grouped by domain, for a menu that fits on one screen.

functions.name: format_card
functions.doc: The card as text, printed or returned. No colour and no box drawing: it survives a pipe.

functions.name: search
functions.sig: (text: str, top: int = 5, *, min_score: float = 0.0) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc:
Rank presets against a free-text description, English or Portuguese.

Returns dicts with ``name``, ``score`` (0-1, relative to the best hit), ``matched`` (the terms
that hit, so the ranking can be judged) and the card fields a caller needs to explain it.

Two things keep it honest: a term counts for more when few presets use it (``crack`` beats
``plane``), and a domain named in the query boosts every preset of that domain (``flow past a
cylinder`` is a fluid problem, whatever else the sentence contains).

children.summary: The preset catalogue: what a preset takes, what it gives back, and the smallest program that uses it.

children.name: pinneapple_core.onboarding.cli
children.doc:
``pinneapple doctor | recommend | card | new``: the four commands a new user needs first.

They are separate from ``pinneapple check`` (which lints results) because they answer questions
about *getting started*, not about a result. All four run offline and print plain text: no colour,
no box drawing, readable in a terminal, a log or a CI transcript.

functions.name: main
functions.doc: ``pinneapple <doctor|recommend|card|new> ...``

children.summary: Pinneapple doctor | recommend | card | new: the four commands a new user needs first.

children.name: pinneapple_core.onboarding.doctor
children.doc:
Is this installation ready for what I want to do? One check per thing, one fix per failure.

``pp.info()`` answers "what is in the library". ``pp.doctor()`` answers the question a new user
actually has, which is narrower and more useful: *for the work I intend to do, is anything
missing?* The intent is named by a profile:

=============  ==========================================================================
profile        for
=============  ==========================================================================
``start``      the first week: solve a preset, plot a field, train one small network
``cfd``        geometry to mesh to an OpenFOAM/CalculiX campaign, plus 3-D viewing
``research``   PINNs, operators, uncertainty, JAX, publication figures
``enterprise`` serving, signatures, the physics linter in CI, the hub and the MCP server
``all``        every extra the package declares
``gpu``        the NVIDIA simulation stack: Newton rigid bodies on Warp, and Warp itself
=============  ==========================================================================

Every failure prints the exact command that fixes it, and nothing is reported as fine when it was
not checked: a check that cannot run says so.

>>> import pinneapple as pp
>>> report = pp.doctor("cfd")          # returns the report and prints it
>>> report.ok                          # True when nothing required is missing

classes.name: Check
classes.doc: One thing that was checked. ``ok`` is None when the check could not run.

functions.name: profiles
functions.doc: The profiles ``doctor`` accepts, with the sentence that describes each one.

functions.name: doctor
functions.doc:
Check this installation against a profile and, with ``verbose``, print the report.

``profile`` is one of :func:`profiles`. Nothing is installed and nothing is downloaded; every
missing item comes with the command that fixes it.

children.summary: Is this installation ready for what I want to do? One check per thing, one fix per failure.

children.name: pinneapple_core.onboarding.newproject
children.doc:
``pp.new`` / ``pinneapple new``: a project a person can grow, outside this repository.

The repository's own scaffold (``python -m pinneapple_lab scaffold``) creates an *example* of the
library, wired into the Lab here. A user needs the opposite: a folder of their own, with no
dependency on this checkout, that runs on a clean install and survives being copied to a colleague.

Three templates, by how much Python the user wants to write:

``plain``
    The user edits ``case.yaml`` and nothing else. ``run.py`` resolves the problem (from a preset
    or from a sentence), solves it with the cheapest method that works, saves the field, a figure,
    and a one-page report. No Python is required to go from "my problem" to "a number and a plot".
``research``
    ``study.py`` solves, compares against the classical answer where one exists, records metrics
    and checks, and writes an experiment manifest the Lab can grade, next to a notebook.
``cfd``
    A campaign runner: one preset, a parameter swept over a list, the reference solver per case,
    a CSV of quantities of interest and a convergence figure, with the geometry hook written down.

Every generated file runs as written on a clean ``pip install pinneapple``; the folders the user
will fill are created; and no path depends on the directory the script was launched from.

>>> import pinneapple as pp
>>> path = pp.new("my_study", template="plain")      # writes ./my_study and prints the next step

functions.name: plan
functions.sig: (name: str, template: str = 'plain', preset: str = 'burgers_1d') -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: What ``new_project`` would write, without writing it. Useful for a dry run and for tests.

functions.name: new_project
functions.sig: (name: str, *, dir: str | None = None, template: str = 'plain', preset: str = 'burgers_1d', verbose: bool = True) -> str
functions.doc:
Write a standalone project and return its folder.

``name``: the folder name, lowercase letters, digits and underscores. ``dir``: the parent
folder, the current directory by default. ``template``: ``plain``, ``research`` or ``cfd``
(see :data:`TEMPLATES`). ``preset``: the problem to start from.

children.summary: Pp.new / pinneapple new: a project a person can grow, outside this repository.

children.name: pinneapple_core.onboarding.recommend
children.doc:
One sentence in, a plan out: which preset, which method, which model, and why.

A new user arrives with a problem, not with a preset name. This module answers the three
questions they actually have, in the order they have them:

1. which preset is closest to my problem (and what do the near ones differ in),
2. which method gives an answer today without training anything,
3. which model to train once the problem description is right.

The ranking is keyword scoring over a curated catalogue (:mod:`pinneapple_core.onboarding.catalog`),
so it can be wrong, and it says how it decided: every recommendation carries the terms that matched
and the terms that did not. When nothing matches, it says so and routes to
``pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.capabilities.suggest_problem_spec`` and to ``pp.new`` instead
of inventing a preset.

classes.name: Recommendation
classes.doc: What to run, why this, and what to run next. ``explain()`` is the text a person reads.

functions.name: recommend
functions.doc:
Turn a problem description into a preset, a method and a model, with the reasons.

Accepts English or Portuguese. Runs offline: no model is trained and nothing is downloaded.

>>> import pinneapple as pp
>>> r = pp.recommend("heat sink cooled by a fan")
>>> r.preset
'fan_cooler_cfd'
>>> print(r.explain())

children.summary: One sentence in, a plan out: which preset, which method, which model, and why.

children.doc:
pinneapple_core.onboarding — the first hour with PINNeAPPle.

Everything a new user needs before writing physics code:

* :func:`~pinneapple_core.onboarding.doctor.doctor` checks the installation against a *profile*
  (``start``, ``cfd``, ``research``, ``enterprise``) and prints one fix command per problem.
* :func:`~pinneapple_core.onboarding.recommend.recommend` turns a problem described in one
  sentence, in English or Portuguese, into a preset, a method and a runnable snippet, and says why.
* :func:`~pinneapple_core.onboarding.catalog.card` prints what a preset takes, what it gives back
  and the smallest program that uses it.
* :func:`~pinneapple_core.onboarding.newproject.new_project` writes a standalone project (not an
  example inside this repository) with a case file, a runner and a README, at three levels of
  programming: ``plain`` (edit a YAML, never touch Python), ``research`` (experiment manifests and
  a notebook) and ``cfd`` (geometry and solver campaigns).

The four are also reachable from the command line as ``pinneapple doctor``, ``pinneapple
recommend``, ``pinneapple card`` and ``pinneapple new``.

>>> import pinneapple as pp
>>> pp.doctor()                       # is this installation ready for what I want to do?
>>> pp.recommend("heat conduction in a fin")   # which preset and method should I start from?
>>> pp.card("burgers_1d")             # what does it take, what does it give back?
>>> pp.new("my_study", template="plain")       # a folder I can grow into a paper or a product
children.summary: The first hour with PINNeAPPle.

children.name: pinneapple_core.ontology
children.doc:
A ontologia física: um tipo formal por conceito, e os três consumidores usando o mesmo (#204).

O mesmo conceito aparecia escrito três vezes na biblioteca, cada vez com o seu formato: um campo era ``spec.fields``
(uma tupla de nomes) no ``ProblemSpec``, um ``Field`` com unidade e localização no manifesto do dataset, e uma linha
de ``inputs``/``outputs`` (um dicionário com ``name``/``unit``) no cartão de modelo. Uma condição de contorno era
``ConditionSpec(kind="dirichlet", value_fn=...)`` no primeiro, ``BoundaryCondition(field, region, kind, value)`` no
segundo e ``boundary_conditions: dict`` no terceiro. Nada disso era falso — o problema é que eram três definições do
mesmo conceito, e três definições divergem.

Este módulo é a definição única. Os treze conceitos do #204 estão aqui como modelos ``pydantic`` com
``extra="forbid"``:

======================  ==========================================================================
conceito                o que fixa
======================  ==========================================================================
``PhysicalSystem``      o agregado: tudo abaixo, com as referências cruzadas conferidas
``Domain``              os eixos do domínio, com unidade e limites (``Axis``)
``Geometry``            a forma e os arquivos que a descrevem, e a unidade em que eles estão
``Material``            um material nomeado com propriedades **com unidade**
``Field``               uma variável: nome, unidade, componentes, eixos e papel
``Parameter``           um parâmetro do caso: valor, unidade, procedência
``GoverningEquation``   a equação que o caso satisfaz, em texto, com os campos e parâmetros que ela usa
``ConstitutiveLaw``     a relação constitutiva, e à qual campo ou equação ela se aplica
``BoundaryCondition``   qual campo, em qual região, de qual tipo, com que valor
``InitialCondition``    o estado inicial de um campo transiente
``Observation``         uma medida do campo, com a incerteza que ela carrega
``Solver``              quem resolve (família e biblioteca), e com que ajustes
``Model``               o que se treinou, o que ele prevê e com que dados
======================  ==========================================================================

As unidades passam pelo mesmo validador do resto da biblioteca (:func:`unit_or_dimensionless`, que é a função que o
esquema do dataset já usava e que agora mora aqui): um ``unit`` que não analisa é erro na construção, não descoberto
quatro camadas depois.

O que a montagem de um :class:`PhysicalSystem` **cobra**, e é o motivo de o agregado existir
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Um conjunto de objetos soltos sempre parece consistente. Juntá-los faz as perguntas chatas:

* a equação governante cita um campo que não está na lista de campos? Erro.
* a condição de contorno aponta para um campo inexistente, ou para uma região vazia? Erro.
* o modelo diz que prevê um campo que o sistema não declara? Erro.
* dois campos com o mesmo nome? Dois parâmetros com o mesmo nome? Erro.
* o eixo que o campo indexa não está no domínio? Erro.
* uma condição de Dirichlet/Neumann/Robin sem valor nem expressão? Erro.

Reuso pelos três consumidores, e onde ele está
----------------------------------------------
* ``ProblemSpec.to_system()`` (:mod:`pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.spec`) — domínio, campos, parâmetros,
  equação, condições e solver do problema;
* ``PhysicsDataBundle`` / ``BundleManifest.physical_system()`` (:mod:`pinneapple_data.schema.bundle`) — o manifesto do
  dataset, e as classes ``Field``/``Parameter``/``BoundaryCondition``/``InitialCondition``/``Material`` do próprio
  esquema do dataset, que agora **herdam** daqui em vez de redefinir;
* ``ModelCard.to_system()`` (:mod:`pinneapple_hub.model_card`) — os ``inputs``/``outputs`` do cartão viram campos
  com unidade analisada, e ``equations``/``boundary_conditions`` viram equação e condições tipadas.

O teste que responde ao aceite de verdade está em ``tests/pinneapple_core/test_ontology.py``: o **mesmo caso**
descrito pelos três caminhos tem de produzir conceitos **iguais** (``Field``, ``Parameter``, ``GoverningEquation``),
não equivalentes em prosa.

Limite declarado: o ``ProblemSpec`` não carrega unidades nesta versão. Quando ele não tem `meta["units"]`, o sistema
gerado marca a unidade como ``"1"`` — dimensão adimensional — em vez de adivinhar ``"m/s"`` pelo nome do campo.

    >>> from pinneapple_core.ontology import Field, GoverningEquation, Parameter, PhysicalSystem
    >>> u = Field(name="u", unit="1", components=["u"], axes=["x"])
    >>> nu = Parameter(name="nu", value=0.01, unit="1")
    >>> system = PhysicalSystem(
    ...     name="burgers",
    ...     fields=[u],
    ...     parameters=[nu],
    ...     governing_equations=[GoverningEquation(name="burgers", expression="u_t + u u_x = nu u_xx",
    ...                                            fields=["u"], parameters=["nu"])],
    ... )
    >>> system.fields[0].unit, len(system.governing_equations)
    ('1', 1)
    >>> Field(name="p", unit="unknown").unit        # "unknown" é uma unidade que existe e não foi anotada
    'unknown'
    >>> Field(name="p", unit="-").unit              # os dois jeitos de escrever adimensional viram um só
    '1'

A unidade é analisada **na construção**: ``Field(name="p", unit="m/s+")`` levanta ``ValueError`` dizendo que
``m/s+`` não é uma unidade que a biblioteca conhece, em vez de deixar o erro aparecer quatro camadas depois.

classes.name: Axis
classes.doc: Um eixo do domínio: o nome (``x``, ``t``), a unidade das suas coordenadas e, quando conhecidos, os limites.

classes.name: Domain
classes.doc: O domínio do sistema: os eixos que o definem, cada um com a sua unidade.

methods.name: bounds
methods.doc: Os limites por eixo; eixo sem limites fica de fora (não é ``(0, 1)`` por omissão).

classes.name: Geometry
classes.doc:
A forma do domínio e os arquivos que a descrevem, com a unidade em que esses arquivos estão.

``units`` é a unidade do arquivo, não a da simulação: um STEP em ``mm`` resolvido em ``m`` registra ``"mm"`` aqui
e ``"m"`` no eixo — é a diferença que some e multiplica um coeficiente de arrasto por ``1e-3``.

classes.name: Material
classes.doc: Um material nomeado com as suas propriedades e a unidade de cada uma.

classes.name: Field
classes.doc:
Uma variável do sistema: nome, unidade, componentes, eixos que ela indexa e o papel que ela tem.

``role`` responde "por que este campo existe no sistema": ``solution`` é o que se resolve, ``input`` é o que se
impõe, ``derived`` é calculado a partir dos outros e ``observed`` é o que se mede.

classes.name: Parameter
classes.doc: Um parâmetro do caso (uma viscosidade, uma condutividade), com a unidade e de onde ele veio.

classes.name: Observation
classes.doc: Uma medida de um campo, e a incerteza que ela carrega (``None`` = não declarada, que não é zero).

classes.name: GoverningEquation
classes.doc:
A equação que o sistema satisfaz, com os campos e parâmetros que ela cita.

``expression`` é o texto da equação (``"u_t + u u_x = nu u_xx"``): este esquema não finge analisar EDPs — quem
faz isso é :mod:`pinneapple_physics.pde_environment` —, ele registra o enunciado para que a checagem a jusante
saiba contra o que está checando.

classes.name: ConstitutiveLaw
classes.doc: A relação constitutiva (``tau = mu du/dy``, ``q = -k grad T``) e a que campo ou equação ela se aplica.

classes.name: BoundaryCondition
classes.doc: Uma condição de contorno: qual campo, em qual região, de qual tipo, com que valor ou expressão.

methods.name: prescribes_something
methods.doc:
A condição diz o que impõe? ``wall``/``symmetry``/``periodic``/``open`` impõem por si; as demais precisam
de valor ou expressão. A checagem é feita pelo sistema, não na construção: um registro do dataset pode ter a
condição ainda não preenchida.

classes.name: InitialCondition
classes.doc: O estado de onde um caso transiente parte.

classes.name: Solver
classes.doc: Quem resolve o sistema: a família numérica, a biblioteca e os ajustes que de fato foram usados.

classes.name: Model
classes.doc: O que se treinou: a família, os campos que ele prevê e sobre o que ele foi treinado.

classes.name: PhysicalSystem
classes.doc:
O sistema físico inteiro, e a hora em que as referências cruzadas são conferidas.

Cada lista é opcional porque um dataset de tabela não tem equação governante e um cartão de modelo não tem malha.
O que não é opcional é a coerência do que está declarado: tudo o que é citado (campo, parâmetro, eixo) tem de
existir no próprio sistema.

methods.name: summary
methods.doc: Quantos objetos de cada conceito o sistema declara — o que se confere antes de comparar dois sistemas.

methods.name: from_problem_spec
methods.doc:
O sistema que um ``ProblemSpec`` descreve. Ver a nota do docstring do módulo sobre unidades: o
``ProblemSpec`` não as carrega, e o que não está em ``spec.meta["units"]`` fica ``"1"`` em vez de adivinhado.

methods.name: from_bundle_manifest
methods.doc: O sistema que o manifesto de um ``PhysicsDataBundle`` descreve (esquema ``pinneapple.physics-data/1``).

methods.name: from_model_card
methods.doc: O sistema que um ``ModelCard`` descreve: os ``inputs``/``outputs`` viram campos com unidade analisada.

functions.name: unit_or_dimensionless
functions.doc:
Devolve ``text`` se for uma unidade analisável, se for uma grafia de adimensional, ou ``"unknown"``.

É a mesma regra que o esquema do dataset aplicava por conta própria; agora mora aqui e os dois lados a importam.
A importação de ``parse_unit`` é feita dentro da função porque ``pinneapple_data`` importa este módulo (pelo
esquema do dataset) — no topo, isso seria um ciclo de importação.

functions.name: json_schema
functions.doc: O esquema JSON de :class:`PhysicalSystem` — o documento que se publica para outros consumidores.

functions.name: publish_schema
functions.doc: Escreve o esquema JSON em ``path`` (o publicado no repositório é ``docs/schemas/physics_ontology.json``).

children.summary: A ontologia física: um tipo formal por conceito, e os três consumidores usando o mesmo (#204).

children.name: pinneapple_core.operators
children.doc:
Physics operators: ``grad, div, curl, laplacian, jacobian, hessian, integrate, flux``.

The ``torch.nn.functional`` of physics: one function per operator that works the same
on a continuous field (a torch callable, derivatives by autograd), on a grid, on a
simplex mesh and on a point cloud (a :class:`~pinneapple_core.Field`).

* On a :class:`Field` the operator takes no point argument and returns a ``Field``
  on the same support (``integrate`` and ``flux`` return numbers).
* On a callable or :class:`FunctionField` it takes the evaluation points ``x`` and
  returns a tensor that keeps the autograd graph.

Shape convention: ``(N,)`` scalar, ``(N, d)`` vector, ``jacobian`` is ``(N, c, d)``
with ``J[n, i, j] = d f_i / d x_j``, ``hessian`` is ``(N, d, d)``.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from pinneapple_core import Field, laplacian
>>> x = np.linspace(0, 1, 41)
>>> u = Field.on_grid([x, x], lambda p: p[:, 0] ** 2 + 3 * p[:, 1] ** 2)
>>> round(float(laplacian(u).values[500]), 6)
8.0

functions.doc: Divergence of a vector field with ``d`` components.

functions.doc: Jacobian ``(N, c, d)``, ``J[n, i, j] = d f_i / d x_j``. A scalar has ``c = 1``.

functions.doc:
Curl of a vector field: a vector in 3D (``(N, 3)``), a scalar in 2D (``(N,)``,
the z component ``dv/dx - du/dy``).

functions.doc: Hessian ``(N, d, d)`` of a scalar field.

functions.name: laplacian
functions.doc:
Sum of second derivatives. A scalar gives a scalar, a vector field applies it
to each component.

functions.name: integrate
functions.doc:
Integral over the field's support (trapezoid on a grid, exact P1 on a mesh,
quadrature or Monte Carlo on a cloud). A continuous field takes ``n=`` samples
(Monte Carlo over its Domain) or ``points=`` and ``weights=``.

functions.name: flux
functions.sig: (f, where: Where = None, *, domain: Optional[Domain] = None, n: int = 20000, seed: int = 0)
functions.doc:
Flux of a vector field out of the boundary, ``integral of f . n dS``.

``where`` restricts it to part of the boundary: a face name of a box (``"x_min"``,
``"x_max"``, ``"y_min"``, ...) or a predicate on boundary points. By the divergence
theorem ``flux(f)`` equals ``integrate(div(f))``.

* Grid: trapezoid over each face (face names only).
* Mesh: exact for P1 fields over the boundary facets.
* Point cloud, or a continuous field: Monte Carlo with ``n`` boundary samples
  of ``domain`` (a continuous field uses its own domain; pass ``domain=`` for a
  cloud). Statistical error ~ 1/sqrt(n).

children.name: pinneapple_core.optim
children.doc:
``PhysicsOptimizer(parameters, objective, constraints)``: one interface for several optimizer families.

>>> import torch
>>> from pinneapple_core.optim import PhysicsOptimizer, ineq
>>> opt = PhysicsOptimizer({"x": (-3, 3), "y": (-3, 3)},
...                        objective=lambda v: (v[0] - 2) ** 2 + (v[1] - 1) ** 2,
...                        constraints=[ineq(lambda v: v[0] + v[1] - 2)])       # x + y <= 2
>>> r = opt.minimize("slsqp")
>>> [round(float(t), 3) for t in r.x]
[1.5, 0.5]

The problem (parameters with bounds, an objective, inequality ``g(x) <= 0`` and equality ``h(x) = 0``
constraints) is written once. ``minimize(method)`` picks the family:

========================  =================================================================  ==========================
method                    what it is                                                          needs
========================  =================================================================  ==========================
``slsqp``                 sequential quadratic programming, autograd gradients               a torch objective
``adjoint``               the same SQP with a gradient you supply (adjoint, implicit solve)   ``grad=``
``penalty``               projected Adam on the objective plus a growing quadratic penalty    a torch objective
``augmented_lagrangian``  projected Adam with multiplier updates (exact constraints)           a torch objective
``differential_evolution`` population search, no gradients                                      nothing
``bayesian``              Gaussian-process expected improvement, for expensive objectives     nothing
========================  =================================================================  ==========================

The objective and constraint functions receive the parameter vector (a float64 torch tensor, or a numpy array
with ``backend="numpy"``; with ``argument="dict"`` a dict of scalars) and return a scalar (constraints may return
a vector). Every method returns the same :class:`OptimizeResult`; ``compare`` runs several on the same problem.
Optimal control and MPC are a separate roadmap item.

Parameters, an objective and constraints, minimised by any of :func:`list_methods`.

Args:
    parameters: ``{name: (lo, hi)}``, ``{name: (lo, hi, x0)}`` or ``{name: {"bounds": (lo, hi), "x0": v}}``.
    objective: ``f(x) -> scalar`` to minimise.
    constraints: :func:`ineq` / :func:`eq` objects (or ``(fn, "ineq"|"eq")`` tuples).
    backend: ``"torch"`` (objective is differentiable by autograd) or ``"numpy"`` (plain function; gradient
        methods then use finite differences).
    argument: ``"vector"`` or ``"dict"``, what the functions receive.
    tol: a point is feasible when every violation is at most ``tol``.

Run ``method`` (see the module table). Options per method: ``max_iter`` (all), ``lr`` / ``rounds`` /
``mu`` (penalty and augmented Lagrangian), ``popsize`` (evolutionary), ``n_initial`` / ``n_candidates``
(bayesian). ``grad(x_numpy) -> gradient`` is required by ``adjoint``.

methods.doc: Run several methods on this problem. ``adjoint`` is skipped unless ``grad=`` is given.

children.name: pinneapple_core.physics_tensor
children.doc:
``PhysicsTensor``: a ``torch.Tensor`` that knows what it is (#186, roadmap item X2).

A value in this library usually has four things attached to it that a plain tensor forgets: a **name**, a **unit**,
the **domain** it was sampled on and what its **components** mean. Losing them is how ``u`` (m/s) ends up added to
``p`` (Pa) and the mistake surfaces three layers later as a bad number. This module keeps them attached and refuses
the operations where they do not fit:

>>> import pinneapple as pp
>>> u = pp.tensor([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], name="velocity", units="m/s", coords=("x", "y"))
>>> u.name, u.units
('velocity', 'm/s')
>>> p = pp.tensor([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], name="pressure", units="Pa")
>>> (u + p).units                                    # doctest: +SKIP
Traceback (most recent call last):
UnitError: cannot add 'm/s' (velocity) to 'Pa' (pressure): the dimensions differ

What it does, exactly:

* ``pp.tensor(...)`` builds one; ``.name``, ``.units``, ``.unit`` (parsed ``Unit``), ``.domain``, ``.coords``,
  ``.components`` and ``.semantics`` read the labels back;
* every ``torch`` operation keeps working and its result **is** a ``PhysicsTensor`` carrying the labels of the first
  labelled operand, so ``u * 2`` and ``u.sum()`` do not drop the unit;
* autograd is untouched -- the result of a labelled operation keeps its ``grad_fn``, and ``loss.backward()`` fills the
  ``.grad`` of a tensor that required grad;
* **additive operations and comparisons between two labelled tensors require the same dimension**
  (``u + p`` and ``u < p`` raise ``UnitError``); adding a plain tensor or a number is allowed and means "same unit";
* multiplying two *dimensioned* tensors is refused rather than guessed: combining ``m/s`` and ``Pa`` correctly needs
  a unit algebra this class does not implement, and a wrong guess is worse than an error. ``.convert("km/h")``
  converts the values to another unit of the same dimension.

Known limit, stated because it is the kind of thing a benchmark finds: the labels are metadata, not a physical type
system. A result computed from ``u`` and ``p`` in a way that goes through an unlabelled tensor (``.numpy()``, a loss
that returns a Python float) comes back unlabelled -- which is honest, since nothing in that path carried the unit.

classes.doc: A tensor with a name, a unit, a domain and component labels. Use :func:`tensor` to build one.

methods.name: semantics
methods.doc: The labels as one dict -- what to record next to a result so the unit is not lost in a log.

methods.name: labelled
methods.doc: Whether anything at all is attached (a tensor with no unit, no name and no domain is just a tensor).

methods.name: without_labels
methods.doc: A plain tensor with the same storage and history -- for a function that does not know about labels.

methods.name: convert
methods.doc: The same physical quantity written in another unit of the same dimension (``km/h`` from ``m/s``).

functions.doc:
``pp.tensor(data, name=..., units=..., domain=...)``: a tensor that remembers what it is (#186).

``units`` is anything :func:`pinneapple_data.physical_units.parse_unit` accepts (``"m/s"``, ``"Pa"``,
``"W/(m·K)"``) or an already parsed ``Unit``; ``domain`` is whatever describes where the values live (a
``Domain``, a mesh, a mapping of bounds -- it is carried, not interpreted here); ``coords`` and ``components``
name the axes. ``requires_grad=True`` makes it a leaf so autograd can fill ``.grad``.

children.name: pinneapple_core.registry
children.doc:
``pp.registry``: one registry protocol for every extensible object type.

The library grew a registry per object type, each with its own shape: presets are a module dict behind a decorator,
solvers are ``solving._METHODS`` with a ``kind`` label, models are ``ModelRegistry`` with a family and a spec,
datasets are a ``DatasetRegistry`` of ``DatasetInfo`` plus a loader, materials are the ``MATERIALS`` dict. This module
gives them one protocol, so a user (and a plugin) learns it once::

    import pinneapple as pp

    pp.register(MySolver, kind="solver", name="my_solver")   # or @pp.register(kind="solver")
    pp.registered("solver")                                  # every name, the ones the library ships included
    pp.resolve("solver", "my_solver")                        # the object itself
    pp.unregister("solver", "my_solver")

Nine kinds: ``physics`` (problem presets), ``model``, ``solver``, ``operator``, ``dataset``, ``benchmark``,
``geometry``, ``material`` and ``optimizer``. Each kind declares what it accepts, once, in :data:`KINDS`; registering
something of the wrong type raises ``WrongType`` naming the kind and what it takes, instead of failing later inside a
solve.

Where a kind already had a home in the library, registering through here also reaches that home — a ``solver`` becomes
callable through ``pp.solve(problem, "my_solver")``, a ``physics`` preset through ``pp.get_preset("my_problem")``, a
``model`` through ``pp.list_models()``, a ``dataset`` through ``DatasetRegistry``, a ``material`` through
``MATERIALS``. ``operator``, ``benchmark``, ``geometry`` and ``optimizer`` had no registry of their own: this module is
where they live, and :func:`resolve` is how the rest of the library (and a plugin) finds them.

Inference is deliberately conservative: ``pp.register(obj)`` without ``kind`` only works when the type settles it — a
``torch.nn.Module`` subclass is a model, a ``Material`` is a material, a ``Geometry`` is a geometry, a ``DatasetInfo``
is a dataset. A plain callable could be a solver, an operator or a benchmark, so it raises ``AmbiguousKind`` and asks
for ``kind=``.

classes.doc: Anything the registry refuses.

classes.name: UnknownKind
classes.doc: ``kind`` is not one of :data:`KINDS`.

classes.name: UnknownName
classes.doc: No object of that kind is registered under that name.

classes.name: AlreadyRegistered
classes.doc: The name is taken in this kind (``replace=True`` overwrites).

classes.name: WrongType
classes.doc: The object does not satisfy what the kind accepts.

classes.name: AmbiguousKind
classes.doc: The type does not settle the kind; pass ``kind=`` explicitly.

classes.name: Registry

A ``name -> object`` map with one validation rule, one error vocabulary and an optional bridge to a legacy home.

``accepts`` is the predicate of the kind, ``accepts_doc`` says in words what it accepts, and ``bridge`` (when the
library already had a home for the kind) is called on the first registration of a name to give it to that home too.

A listener never breaks a registration: an exception it raises is swallowed and it is dropped from the list, so a
watcher cannot make ``pp.register`` fail.

functions.doc: ``with observe(fn): ...`` — listen for the duration of the block, and remove the listener even on a raise.

children.name: pinneapple_core.reproducibility
children.doc:
Reproducibility: the settings a run needs, the environment it ran in, and the check that it did.

A number is reproducible when a second run of the same code, on the same machine,
with the same seed, gives the same result — or when the difference is measured
and written down. Two things make that fail quietly: a seed that was never set
for one of the three random generators (Python, NumPy, PyTorch), and an
environment that changed without anybody noticing.

``deterministic`` fixes the first, ``environment_fingerprint`` records the
second, and ``run_twice`` measures the difference instead of assuming there is
none. None of them guesses: a run that is not reproducible is reported as such,
with the fields that differ.

The fingerprint is JSON-able on purpose, so it travels inside a run record and
can be compared six months later. It records the settings that were actually in
force, not the ones the caller wishes were.

Example
-------
>>> from pinneapple_core.reproducibility import deterministic, run_twice
>>> with deterministic(seed=0):
...     report = run_twice(train_one_step)
>>> report.identical
True

classes.name: ReproducibilityReport
classes.doc: What two runs of the same callable had to say about each other.

functions.name: seed_everything
functions.doc:
Seed Python, NumPy and PyTorch, and return what was set.

The returned record is meant to go into the run record: it is the evidence
that the seed was applied, not a claim that it was.

functions.name: deterministic
functions.sig: (seed: int = 0, *, strict: bool = True, warn_only: bool = False)
functions.doc:
Run the block with the seeds set and the deterministic algorithms on.

``strict`` turns on ``torch.use_deterministic_algorithms``, which makes an
operation without a deterministic implementation raise instead of silently
returning a different answer. ``warn_only`` keeps that as a warning — the
honest middle ground when a model uses an operation PyTorch cannot make
deterministic, and the caller needs the run to finish anyway.

Everything is restored on exit, so a deterministic block inside a test does
not leave the process in a state that changes the next test.

functions.name: environment_fingerprint
functions.doc:
The environment a run happened in, as JSON-able values.

Only what the process can actually read: versions of the packages that
change numerical results, the platform, the CPU count and the GPU names.
A field the interpreter does not expose is ``None``, never a guess.

functions.name: compare_results
functions.sig: (first, second, *, atol: float = 0.0, rtol: float = 0.0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Compare two results, returning the verdict and the worst difference.

Numeric content is compared with ``atol``/``rtol``; anything else (labels,
strings, objects without numbers) only has to be equal to itself.

functions.name: run_twice
functions.sig: (fn: Callable[[], Any], *, seed: int = 0, atol: float = 0.0, rtol: float = 0.0, strict: bool = True, fields: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> ReproducibilityReport
functions.doc:
Call ``fn`` twice under the same seed and report whether the results match.

``fields`` narrows the comparison to the named keys when ``fn`` returns a
mapping; by default every key is compared. A field that cannot be compared
numerically is reported as not scored, never silently counted as equal.

functions.name: fingerprint_json
functions.sig: (fingerprint: dict[str, Any] | None = None, indent: int = 2) -> str
functions.doc: The fingerprint as JSON, for a run record.
